oneSentence: These words describe how training data is split and revisited: one example at a time, in small groups, and across full passes through the dataset.
plainExplanation:
When a model learns from examples, the training data does not always go through all at once. A batch is a group of training examples processed together. A mini-batch is just a batch that is smaller than the whole dataset; in practice, most modern training uses mini-batches, so people often say “batch” when they mean “mini-batch”.

An iteration usually means one parameter update step. In that step, the model takes one batch, makes predictions for those examples, compares them with the target signal, computes an error, and adjusts its internal numbers, called parameters. What goes in is one batch of examples, often with features and labels in supervised learning. What comes out is an updated model.

An epoch means one full pass through the entire training dataset. If a dataset has 1,000 examples and the batch size is 100, one epoch contains 10 iterations. If the batch size is 1, that is often called online or stochastic training, and one epoch contains 1,000 iterations. If the batch size is 1,000, one epoch contains 1 iteration.

These terms are related but not interchangeable. Batch size tells you how many examples are used per update. Iteration tells you how many update steps have happened. Epoch tells you how many times the full dataset has been seen. People sometimes use the words loosely, so it helps to check which definition a course, paper or software library is using.

everydayAnalogy.title: Tuning a radio station in small adjustments
everydayAnalogy.story: Amina is tuning a radio to get a clear signal during a long drive. She does not listen to the whole programme before touching the dial again. Instead, she listens for a few seconds, notices the static, makes a small adjustment, then listens to the next few seconds and adjusts again. After she has sampled short sections from the whole programme once, that is like one full pass; if the signal is still not clear enough, she repeats the cycle.

mapping.analogyElement: a few seconds of audio checked at one time

mapping.analogyElement: one small turn of the tuning dial

mapping.analogyElement: sampling short sections across the whole programme once

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A radio signal already exists, and Amina is adjusting a receiver to match it. In model training, the parameters are changed using mathematical gradients from many examples, not by human listening. Also, batches are usually selected from stored data, often shuffled, rather than arriving as fixed time slices of a broadcast.

visual.title: How batch, iteration and epoch fit together
visual.learningObjective: After viewing, the reader should be able to explain that one iteration uses one batch for one update, and one epoch is the set of iterations needed to cover the whole training dataset once.
visual.description: Show a dataset of 12 examples split into 3 batches of 4. Read left to right: each batch feeds one update step, and all three updates together make one epoch. Then show the sequence repeating for epoch 2, with the same count structure but a note that order may be shuffled.

steps.label: Full dataset
steps.explanation: Start with the complete training set, shown as 12 example cards.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw 12 small rectangles in one container labelled “training data: 12 examples”. Number them 1 to 12.

steps.label: Split into batches
steps.explanation: Choose a batch size of 4, so the 12 examples are processed as 3 batches.
steps.visualInstruction: Group the 12 rectangles into three outlined groups of four, labelled “batch 1”, “batch 2”, and “batch 3”.

steps.label: One iteration
steps.explanation: For each batch, the model makes predictions, calculates error, and updates parameters once.
steps.visualInstruction: From each batch, draw an arrow to a box labelled “forward pass + error + update”. Under each arrow, label “1 iteration”.

steps.label: One epoch
steps.explanation: After all 3 batches have been used once, the model has completed one epoch.
steps.visualInstruction: Bracket the three iteration boxes together with a label above: “1 epoch = 3 iterations here”.

steps.label: Repeat if needed
steps.explanation: Training usually continues for multiple epochs, often with examples reshuffled between epochs.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a second row for “epoch 2” with the same 12 examples in a different order and the same three-batch structure. Add a small note: “same data, new pass”.

visual.interaction: On hover or tap, highlight one batch and show the formula: iterations per epoch = number of examples divided by batch size, rounded up when needed.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram explains the relationship between dataset size, batch size, iteration and epoch using 12 training examples. First, 12 examples are shown as the full dataset. Next, they are divided into three batches of four examples each. Each batch goes through one update step, labelled as one iteration. Because there are three batches, there are three iterations in total. A bracket groups those three iterations and labels them as one epoch, meaning one complete pass through all 12 examples. A second row shows epoch 2, where the same 12 examples appear again, possibly in a different order, to show that another epoch repeats the process over the full dataset.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static two-row diagram. Row one shows 12 examples split into 3 batches, each batch connected to one update step, with a brace marking all 3 updates as epoch 1. Row two repeats the same structure for epoch 2 with the example order changed.

workedExample.scenario: Training a classifier to sort short customer messages into “billing”, “delivery” or “other”.
workedExample.input: 1,200 labelled training messages, batch size 100, train for 5 epochs.
process: The 1,200 messages are divided into 12 batches of 100 messages each.
In iteration 1, the model processes batch 1, compares its predictions with the labels, and updates its parameters once.
After 12 iterations, every training message has been used once, so epoch 1 is complete.
The same 1,200 messages are used again for epochs 2 to 5, often in a new order each time.
After 5 epochs, the model has made 60 update steps in total because 12 iterations per epoch times 5 epochs equals 60.
workedExample.result: The training run finishes after 5 full passes through the data and 60 parameter updates; the final model can then be evaluated on validation or test data.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN analytics team is testing a model to identify broad protection-related trends across incident reports that have already been approved for secure internal analysis.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Understanding epoch, batch and iteration helps the team estimate training time, choose hardware settings, and interpret progress reports such as loss changing after each iteration or each epoch.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not upload confidential, personal, survivor, witness, security-sensitive or operational incident data into an unapproved public AI service; use only approved secure environments with human oversight and data protection controls.

whyItMatters: These words affect time, cost, stability and quality during training. If you hear that a model trained for 20 epochs, that does not tell you much unless you also know the batch size and dataset size. A small batch can make updates noisier but sometimes helps generalisation; a very large batch can be efficient on some hardware but may need different learning settings. Iteration counts matter for progress monitoring, while epoch counts matter for judging how many times the model has revisited the data. For non-specialists reviewing a project, these terms help you ask better questions: How many examples were used per update? How many full passes were made? Was the model checked on validation data, or did it simply train for more epochs and risk overfitting?

commonMisconceptions.misconception: An epoch, a batch and an iteration are three words for the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They measure different parts of training. A batch is the group of examples used together. An iteration is one update step using one batch. An epoch is the collection of iterations needed to use the full training dataset once. They are linked, but they are not interchangeable.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: More epochs always mean a better model.
commonMisconceptions.correction: More epochs mean the model sees the training data more times, but performance on new data may stop improving or even get worse. That is why teams watch validation results, not just training progress. Extra epochs can lead to overfitting, where the model matches the training set too closely.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Batch size only changes speed, not learning behaviour.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Batch size affects both computation and the pattern of updates. Smaller batches usually produce noisier gradient estimates, which can change convergence behaviour and sometimes help or hurt generalisation. Larger batches can be more hardware-efficient, but they may require different learning rates or schedules.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: One iteration means one example was processed.
commonMisconceptions.correction: That is only true when batch size is 1. In most modern systems, one iteration uses many examples at once, often tens, hundreds or more, depending on the task and hardware.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Think of training as studying from a large stack of examples. A batch is one small pile you look at at a time. An iteration is one study-and-adjust step using that pile. An epoch is finishing the whole stack once.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Let a training set contain N examples and let batch size be B. In mini-batch gradient-based training, each iteration performs a forward pass on one batch, computes a loss, backpropagates gradients, and updates parameters once. An epoch is one complete pass through the training set, so it takes about N/B iterations per epoch, or ceil(N/B) if the last batch is smaller. In practice, data are often shuffled between epochs. The terms are also used somewhat differently across tools: some logs report progress by iteration or step, others by epoch, and some use “batch” loosely to mean any update unit. These terms describe training procedure, not inference. They also do not by themselves tell you whether the learning is supervised, self-supervised or another training setup.

keyTakeaway: Batch size sets how many examples are used per update, an iteration is one update, and an epoch is enough iterations to cover the full training set once.

quickCheck.question: A dataset has 10,000 training examples and batch size 500. If the model trains for 4 epochs, how many iterations happen in total?
options: 20 iterations, because 10,000 divided by 500 is 20 and that already includes all 4 epochs
40 iterations, because 4 epochs means 10 iterations per epoch
80 iterations, because each epoch has 20 iterations and 4 epochs make 80
2000 iterations, because each example creates one iteration
quickCheck.explanation: With 10,000 examples and batch size 500, each epoch has 20 iterations. Training for 4 epochs means 20 times 4, which equals 80 iterations. This shows why epoch count alone is not enough; you also need batch size and dataset size.
